                    ### Question
                    A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of right-sided facial weakness and sound intolerance. Three days ago, he hit the right side of his head in a motor vehicle collision. He neither lost consciousness nor sought medical attention. Physical examination shows drooping of the mouth and ptosis on the right side. Sensation over the face is not impaired. Impedance audiometry shows an absence of the acoustic reflex in the right ear. Which of the following muscles is most likely paralyzed in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Tensor tympani
opb. Stylopharyngeus
opc. Cricothyroid
opd. Anterior belly of the digastric
ope. Stylohyoid

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's right-sided facial weakness, ptosis, and absence of the acoustic reflex suggest involvement of the facial nerve (CN VII) and potentially the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The facial nerve innervates muscles of facial expression, including those responsible for eyelid closure, which explains the ptosis. The tensor tympani muscle, responsible for dampening sound, is innervated by the trigeminal nerve. However, the absence of the acoustic reflex indicates that the tensor tympani is likely affected due to the injury, but it is not innervated by the facial nerve. The most likely paralyzed muscle in this context, given the facial weakness and ptosis, is the anterior belly of the digastric, which is innervated by the trigeminal nerve. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is that the anterior belly of the digastric is the muscle most likely paralyzed in this patient.
